subject: physics
title: Internal energy and energy transfers
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Internal energy and energy transfers — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.3.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Internal energy and energy transfers, specification section 4.3.2.
final_note: You worked through Internal energy and energy transfers — 24 specification statements.

concepts.def: The energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up that system. It is a store held by the particles, not a fluid that enters or leaves the system.
The energy the particles have because they are moving, vibrating or rotating. It is one of the two contributions to internal energy, and it is the contribution linked to temperature.

The energy stored because of the positions of the particles relative to one another and the forces between them. It is the second contribution to internal energy, and it is the store that changes during a change of state.
An energy transfer that increases the energy of the particles that make up a system. The result is either a rise in the temperature of the system or a change of state.
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ. It applies when heating or cooling changes the temperature of a substance.
Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; temperature change, ∆θ, is in degrees Celsius, °C.
Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, because it is an energy quoted for each kilogram and for each degree Celsius of temperature change.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
A change between solid, liquid and vapour in which the substance stays the same substance. While it happens the temperature does not change, even though energy is still being transferred.
The energy needed for a substance to change state. It changes the energy stored (internal energy) of the substance but not its temperature.
The amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature. Energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, or E = m L.
Energy, E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, is in joules per kilogram, J/kg. No temperature unit appears because the temperature does not change.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from solid to liquid, that is for melting, and in reverse for freezing.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from liquid to vapour, that is for boiling, and in reverse for condensing.

A graph of temperature against time for a substance heated or cooled at a steady rate. Sloping sections show the temperature changing within one state; flat sections show a change of state, where energy is still transferred but the temperature is constant.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?
options: The energy stored inside the system by its own particles
The temperature the system reaches when it is heated
The heat that flowed in and is now held inside
The energy the system gives out to its surroundings
mcqs.explain: Energy is stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up the system, and that store is called internal energy.

mcqs.q: Internal energy is the total of which two energy stores of the particles in a system?
options: The chemical energy and the thermal energy of all the particles
The kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles
The kinetic energy of every one of the particles, only
The kinetic energy stored as the particles move about
mcqs.explain: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.

mcqs.q: Where does the potential energy part of a system's internal energy come from?
options: From the speeds at which the particles are moving about inside
From the height of the system above the floor of the laboratory
From the positions of particles and the forces between them
From the temperature the system has been raised to
mcqs.explain: Particles attract one another, so energy is stored in how they are arranged; that is the potential energy part.

mcqs.q: Heating a system increases the energy of the particles that make it up. Which pair of outcomes does the specification give for this?
options: It always raises the temperature of the system, without exception
It raises the temperature and it always changes state as well
It raises the pressure or else it produces a change of state
It raises the temperature or it produces a change of state
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification states: heating either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state.

mcqs.q: A beaker of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater until all the ice has melted. What does the heating do during that time?
options: It raises the temperature of the ice steadily as it melts
It increases the energy stored and produces a change of state
The energy stored stays the same as the temperature holds steady
It has no effect until the ice reaches its melting point
mcqs.explain: The energy supplied increases the energy of the particles and produces the change of state from solid to liquid.

mcqs.q: When a substance is heated and its temperature increases, the size of that increase depends on which three things?
options: The volume, the type of material and the total time of heating
The mass, the final temperature and the energy supplied
The mass, the type of material and the energy input to it
The mass, the energy input and the type of container
mcqs.explain: These are the three factors the specification lists for the increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil are each supplied with 20 000 J. The oil ends up much hotter than the water. Why?
options: Equal masses given equal energy must reach equal temperatures
The oil has a much higher specific heat capacity than water
The oil is thicker, so the heater warms it up quickly
Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than the water does
mcqs.explain: The increase in temperature depends on the type of material; oil needs less energy per kilogram per degree Celsius.

mcqs.q: Which word equation for the change in thermal energy is the one given in the specification?
options: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × the final temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat × the temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ the temperature change
mcqs.explain: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ.

mcqs.q: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what do the symbols c and ∆θ stand for?
options: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the final temperature
c is the specific latent heat and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the capacity of the container and ∆θ is a state change
mcqs.explain: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, c is specific heat capacity in J/kg °C and ∆θ is the temperature change in °C.

mcqs.q: In which of these situations does the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ apply?
options: While ice at 0 °C melts into water that is also at 0 °C
While water at 100 °C is boiling away steadily into steam
While water at 0 °C freezes solid inside a freezer
While the water in a kettle warms from 20 °C up to 90 °C
mcqs.explain: The temperature of the water is changing with no change of state, which is when ∆E = m c ∆θ applies.

mcqs.q: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, which units does the specification give for ∆E and for ∆θ?
options: ∆E is in joules, J, and ∆θ is in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules per second, and ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in joules per kilogram, J/kg
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in J/kg °C
mcqs.explain: The specification gives change in thermal energy, ∆E, in joules, J, and temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius, °C.

mcqs.q: A student uses ∆E = m c ∆θ for a 250 g block of aluminium. What should be substituted for m?
options: 250, because that is the mass given in the question
0.25, because the mass must be in kilograms
2.50, because grams are converted by dividing by 100
250 000, since kilograms are the larger unit here
mcqs.explain: Mass, m, is in kilograms, so 250 g is divided by 1000 to give 0.25 kg.

mcqs.q: What are the units of specific heat capacity, and why does a temperature appear in them?
options: J/kg, because the value is quoted for one kilogram of substance
J/°C, because the value is quoted for one degree Celsius
J/kg °C, because the substance is heated for one whole minute
J/kg °C, because the value fixes one kilogram and a one degree rise
mcqs.explain: Specific heat capacity, c, is in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, matching its definition.

mcqs.q: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The energy required to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
The energy required to raise the whole of the sample by one degree Celsius
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of it
The energy stored by one kilogram of it at a given temperature
mcqs.explain: This is the definition: the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

mcqs.q: Blocks P and Q have the same mass. P has the higher specific heat capacity. The same energy is supplied to each block. What happens?
options: P has the greater temperature rise, because its capacity is larger
Q has the greater temperature rise, needing less energy per °C
Both rise by the same amount, since the energy supplied is equal
Q must change state first, because its capacity is smaller
mcqs.explain: Q needs fewer joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, so the same energy raises its temperature more.

mcqs.q: 10 500 J are supplied to 0.50 kg of water, which does not boil. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the temperature change?
10 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy?
What is meant by the latent heat of a substance?
options: The energy stored by a substance once it has melted
The energy that is needed for a substance to change state
The energy needed to raise a substance by one degree
The energy lost by a substance while its temperature is constant
mcqs.explain: The specification calls the energy needed for a substance to change state its latent heat.

mcqs.q: Steam is produced steadily from boiling water at 100 °C. What happens to the energy that is supplied?
options: It raises the temperature of the water past 100 °C
It is stored in the heater until the boiling has finished
It changes the energy stored but not the temperature
It leaves the water's own internal energy unchanged
mcqs.explain: During a change of state the energy supplied changes the internal energy of the substance, not its temperature.

mcqs.q: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts at constant temperature?
options: Their kinetic energy, because the particles must be moving faster
Their thermal energy, as heat flows into the solid and is stored
Neither store, because the temperature is not changing at all
Their potential energy, as the particles are pulled apart
mcqs.explain: The energy supplied separates the particles against the forces between them, raising their potential energy store.

mcqs.q: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific latent heat of a substance?
options: The energy needed to change the state of a whole sample of it
The energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
The energy needed to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
The energy needed to change one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
mcqs.explain: This is the definition: the energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.

mcqs.q: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state?
options: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat × ∆θ
energy for a state change = mass ÷ specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific heat capacity
mcqs.explain: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as E = m L.

mcqs.q: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 330 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.30 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C?
In E = m L, which units does the specification give for the three quantities?
options: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram per °C
E in joules, m in grams, L in joules per kilogram of substance
E in joules per second, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
mcqs.explain: The specification gives energy, E, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, in joules per kilogram, J/kg.

mcqs.q: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of fusion describe?
options: The change of state from liquid to vapour, that is boiling
The change of state from a solid straight to a vapour
The change of state from a solid to a liquid, that is melting
The change of state from liquid into a warmer liquid
mcqs.explain: The specification gives specific latent heat of fusion as the change of state from solid to liquid.

mcqs.q: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of vaporisation describe?
options: The change of state from a solid straight into a gas
The change of state from solid to liquid
The rise in temperature of the vapour formed
The change of state from a liquid to a vapour
mcqs.explain: The specification gives specific latent heat of vaporisation as the change of state from liquid to vapour.

mcqs.q: A solid is heated at a steady rate and a graph of temperature against time is plotted. What does a flat section of the graph show?
options: The substance is changing state while energy is supplied
The substance has reached the hottest temperature it can ever reach
The heater has been switched off, so no energy is transferred
The substance is warming too slowly for the thermometer
mcqs.explain: A flat section means constant temperature: the energy supplied is producing the change of state.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes specific heat capacity from specific latent heat?
options: They are two names for one quantity, so either may be used for any change
Specific heat capacity needs a temperature change; latent heat does not
Specific heat capacity changes state; specific latent heat changes temperature
Either quantity may be used for any thermal change at all
mcqs.explain: c is the energy per kilogram per degree Celsius of temperature change; L is the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature.
